title: Designing a Time-Based Key-Value Store

phrases.phrase: at or before a given timestamp
phrases.explanation: Find the value whose timestamp is equal to or less than the specified time

technical_terms.definition: An algorithm that finds a target in a sorted collection by repeatedly halving the search range
A sorted map implementation in Java backed by a red-black tree, supporting efficient range queries
A data structure that maps keys to values with average O of one lookup time

concept: Design a data structure that supports two operations: set(key, value, timestamp) stores the key-value pair at the given timestamp, and get(key, timestamp) returns the value associated with the key at the largest timestamp less than or equal to the given timestamp. If no such timestamp exists, return an empty string.

solutions.label: Linear Scan with HashMap
solutions.summary: Store all key-value-timestamp triples in a list per key, then scan linearly for each get query.

solutions.label: Binary Search with Sorted List
solutions.summary: Since timestamps are inserted in increasing order, use binary search on the timestamp list to find the correct value efficiently.

solutions.label: TreeMap for Built-in Floor Lookup
solutions.summary: Use a TreeMap per key so floorKey gives the answer directly with clean, concise code.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Today I'd like you to design a time-based key-value store. It supports two operations. Set stores a key, a value, and a timestamp. Get takes a key and a timestamp and returns the value with the largest timestamp that is less than or equal to the given timestamp. If no such entry exists, return an empty string.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. So for get, I'm looking for the most recent value at or before the requested time. A couple of questions: are timestamps always positive integers, and can set be called multiple times with the same key but different timestamps?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes, timestamps are positive integers. And importantly, for each key the timestamps in set calls are strictly increasing. So you'll never receive an older timestamp after a newer one for the same key. The same key can have many entries at different times.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: That's helpful. The strictly increasing property means the timestamps per key are already sorted. Let me confirm with an example. If I call set with foo, bar, one, then set with foo, baz, three, then get foo at timestamp two should return bar, and get foo at timestamp four should return baz. Correct?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Exactly right. And if you call get with a timestamp smaller than any stored timestamp for that key, return an empty string.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Understood. So I need a data structure mapping each key to its timestamped values, then an efficient way to find the right value for a given timestamp. Let me start with a straightforward approach.

sections.title: Linear Scan with HashMap
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    style H fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style L1 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style L2 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style L3 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style SC fill:#93c5fd,color:#000
    H["HashMap: key='foo'"]
    L1["(1,'bar')"]
    L2["(3,'baz')"]
    L3["(5,'qux')"]
    SC["get('foo',4): scan from end → (3,'baz') ✓"]
    H --> L1 --> L2 --> L3
    L3 --> SC

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: For the brute force, I'll use a HashMap where each key maps to a list of timestamp-value pairs. Set just appends to the list. For get, I scan the list from the end and return the first value whose timestamp is at or before the target.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What's the time complexity of that approach?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Set is O of one since we just append. But get is O of n in the worst case, where n is the number of entries for that key. If the target timestamp is very small, we might scan the entire list before finding a match or reaching the beginning.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Right. That linear scan could be slow if there are millions of entries per key. Can you do better, especially given that timestamps are already sorted?

sections.title: Binary Search with Sorted List
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    style A fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style B fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style C fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style M1 fill:#c4b5fd,color:#000
    style M2 fill:#c4b5fd,color:#000
    style R fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    A["Timestamps: [1, 3, 5]"]
    B["get('foo', 4)"]
    M1["mid=3, 3 ≤ 4 → go right"]
    M2["mid=5, 5 > 4 → go left"]
    C["Search range exhausted"]
    R["Result: timestamp 3 → 'baz'"]
    A --> B --> M1 --> M2 --> C --> R

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Since timestamps per key are strictly increasing, the list is already sorted. I can use binary search on the timestamps. For get with foo at timestamp four, I search the list one, three, five. The midpoint is three, which is less than or equal to four, so I move right. Next I check five, which exceeds four, so I move left. The answer is timestamp three with value baz.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Nice. So you're finding the rightmost timestamp that doesn't exceed the target. What's the complexity now?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Set is still O of one. Get is now O of log n because binary search halves the search space each step. Space is O of n to store all entries. This is a big improvement for large datasets.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great. Is there a way to make the code even cleaner using built-in data structures?

sections.title: TreeMap for Built-in Floor Lookup
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    style T fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style N1 fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style N2 fill:#fdba74,color:#000
    style N3 fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style F fill:#fdba74,color:#000
    T["TreeMap for key='foo'"]
    N2["1 → 'bar'"]
    N1["3 → 'baz'"]
    N3["5 → 'qux'"]
    F["floorEntry(4) → (3,'baz') ✓"]
    T --> N1
    N1 --> N2
    N1 --> N3
    N3 --> F

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: In Java, I can map each key to a TreeMap of timestamp to value. For set, I insert into the TreeMap. For get, I call floorEntry with the target timestamp, which returns the entry with the greatest key less than or equal to the target. It does the binary search internally using a red-black tree.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: How does the complexity compare to your previous solution?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Both set and get are O of log n, and space is O of n. The time complexity matches the binary search approach, but the code is much cleaner. We rely on floorEntry instead of writing our own binary search, reducing the chance of off-by-one errors.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: One trade-off to note: set was O of one with a list but is O of log n with a TreeMap due to tree insertion. In practice, if sets vastly outnumber gets, the list plus binary search approach might be preferable.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: That's a great point. The list approach gives O of one for set at the cost of a manual binary search for get, while the TreeMap gives a clean API but O of log n for both. Choosing depends on the workload pattern.

sections.title: Summary
sections.diagram:
graph LR
    style A fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style B fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style C fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    A["Linear Scan\nSet: O(1) Get: O(n)"]
    B["Binary Search\nSet: O(1) Get: O(log n)"]
    C["TreeMap\nSet: O(log n) Get: O(log n)"]
    A -->|"sort is free"| B
    B -->|"cleaner API"| C

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Good work. You progressed from a linear scan to binary search by recognizing the sorted timestamp property, then simplified the code with a TreeMap. The key insight was that monotonically increasing timestamps give you a sorted structure for free.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Exactly. The linear approach works but is slow for get. Binary search on the sorted list brings get down to O of log n. And the TreeMap approach achieves the same complexity with cleaner code, though set becomes O of log n. Knowing your read-write ratio helps pick the best option.
